biggest_risk: Your largest exposure would be the stretch of self-funded years between leaving work and the start of government benefits, when the portfolio alone would have to carry the full household spending target with no guaranteed-income floor beneath it.
best_lever: Staying on the job for a further stretch is the single move that lifts the plan the most, because each added year keeps contributions flowing while shortening the span the savings must cover.
snapshot_intro: Your plan lands in solid middle ground, succeeding in a good share of tested paths with clear room to firm it up further. The effort you have already put in is the foundation everything else builds on, and this assessment is meant as a starting point rather than a verdict. The result reflects thousands of tested scenarios, including severe crashes and prolonged inflation, yet it cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative change, a major health event, or a separation.
mirror_block: You are roughly a decade out from your planned retirement, with a partner close behind you, and together you have built a substantial pool of savings across registered and non-registered accounts. Most of your future income would come from your own portfolio and your rental properties, with government benefits arriving later and covering only a slice of the household target. The piece that needs the most attention is the early retirement window, where your savings would do the heavy lifting before any government cheque appears.
revenue_analysis: The income you would replace in retirement covers most of what you earn today, which would let your day-to-day life carry on with little visible change. Because so much of that replacement leans on your own portfolio and rental income rather than a guaranteed pension, the steadiness of your lifestyle would track the steadiness of those sources. That structure could hold up well as long as withdrawals stay in step with what the portfolio can sustain.
gov_explanation: Government benefits would form a dependable floor under your retirement, but a floor that covers only a minority of what your household plans to spend. The years before those benefits begin are a distinct phase: during the bridge your savings alone carry the load, and only later does the guaranteed floor step in to ease the draw on your portfolio. That sequencing means your plan leans most heavily on invested capital in its earliest retirement years.
longevity_analysis: Across the tested paths, your wealth at the cautious end of the likely range still leaves a real cushion, while the upper end of that range points to a far larger estate. The gap between those two outcomes reflects how much the order and size of future returns can shape where you land. You can hover over the projection to see how the likely range widens at each age.
priority_actions: What matters most for you is the relationship between your planned spending and what your portfolio can reliably produce in the early retirement years, because that is where the plan is tightest before government income arrives. Easing the spending target during the bridge years could buy meaningful breathing room and stretch how long the savings comfortably last. None of this starts from a position of weakness: your contributions are strong, your accounts are diversified, and the savings already in place give you a solid base to adjust from.
tax_analysis: Your effective tax rate would sit only slightly higher in retirement than it does today, so the shift in what you keep after tax would be small year over year. That gentle step up reflects the move from earned income to portfolio and rental income rather than any sharp change in your bracket. The takeaway is that taxes are a steady background cost here, not a swing factor.
estate_analysis: The median path leaves a sizeable estate, while the cautious tail shows scenarios where little remains. With a balanced preference between enjoying your retirement and leaving something behind, that spread fits comfortably: it suggests room to spend without fear of leaving nothing, while the stronger paths would still pass on a meaningful legacy.
obs_1: **Bridge window** : The years between your retirement and the first government cheque ask your savings to fund the entire household target on their own, and that self-funded draw is the heaviest single demand the plan faces before any guaranteed income arrives to share the load.
obs_2: **Rental income** : Your two rental properties produce a stream of pre-tax rental income that could soften how hard your portfolio has to work each year, easing withdrawal pressure during the bridge, though it is rental income rather than guaranteed net cash flow and would swing with vacancies, repairs, and tenant turnover.
obs_3: **Property concentration** : A large share of your net worth sits in real estate that the plan never sells, so while it anchors your balance sheet it cannot be tapped to cover a shortfall without unwinding a property, which leaves your liquid savings doing the work the bricks cannot.
obs_4: **Two-phase coverage** : Once both of you have begun your government benefits, that guaranteed income covers a minority of the household target for life, but the years beforehand carry little to none of it, so the plan is best read as two distinct phases rather than one steady level of coverage.
obs_5: **Effort versus outcome** : Your savings discipline is among the strongest the model sees, yet the result lands only in the middle, and the tension is that the limit here is less about how much you set aside and more about the size of the spending target the portfolio must support across a long retirement.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years just before retirement could be the most impactful window for shaping how your spending target and your savings line up, since adjustments made now would compound across the whole retirement. The next update of this assessment, in a year, would measure how those choices have moved the plan.
model_blind_spots: The model does not assume any pension income splitting between you and your partner, which could lower the household tax bill and is worth weighing for a couple like yours. It also keeps your primary home untouched, so a future sale of that property would change the liquidity picture entirely, and it cannot anticipate life events such as an inheritance, a career change, or a separation. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
couple_analysis: As a couple retiring within reach of each other, the order in which you draw from each set of accounts and how you spread income across your brackets would shape how much the household keeps after tax. The two survivor paths differ: if you were to pass first, your partner would keep their own benefits plus a survivor portion of yours and receive the tax-free account transfer, while the household's income would step down to a single set of payments. If your partner were to go first, you would retain the registered accounts, and the savings each of you brings makes either trajectory more resilient than a single earner would face alone.
property_analysis: Your primary home carries a remaining mortgage, and the plan never schedules its sale, so its equity stays on the sidelines rather than funding retirement. Together with the rental holdings, a large portion of your wealth is tied up in property that cannot be drawn on quickly, which gives the balance sheet weight but leaves your liquid savings to handle the year-to-year demands. That standby role is fine as long as the portfolio can carry the spending on its own.
savings_analysis: Your accumulation is climbing on the strength of steady monthly contributions paired with a long runway to retirement, and that combination is the main engine carrying your capital upward. The trajectory shows that the discipline already in place does most of the work, which means the plan rewards consistency more than any single dramatic move. The key takeaway is that the path is rising, and protecting the contribution habit would matter more than chasing a higher return.
what_if_analysis: Among the tested scenarios, working longer moves the needle on success more than any other, lifting the plan well above where it sits today. That tells you the plan is most sensitive to the length of the accumulation runway, far more than to the timing of when you claim government benefits, which barely shifts the outcome.
strategy_comparison: Of the paths compared against the status quo, working longer stands out as the one that both raises the success rate and grows median wealth the most, while saving more or delaying government benefits leave the result close to where it already sits. The lesson is that added time in the workforce does heavier lifting here than rearranging the existing pieces.
fees_analysis: Your investment fees are unusually light, so the lifetime cost they drain off the plan amounts to only a small fraction of your retirement income rather than the years-long bite many portfolios suffer. With the vehicle unknown, confirming the structure would be the main loose end, but the drag itself is not what holds this plan back.
